paragraphs.text: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in COL9A3. In a review of patients with biallelic COL9A3 loss-of-function variants, Rad et al. (2022) found that moderate-to-profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss and moderate to high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration were consistent features. Retinal detachment and cataract occurred occasionally, and skeletal involvement, such as spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, seemed more variable.

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) reported a boy of Indian ancestry, born to consanguineous parents who were third cousins, with Stickler syndrome. He failed his newborn hearing screen and had moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss, with mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. His speech delay was attributed to the hearing loss. He had progressive high myopia but no vitreous abnormalities or retinal degeneration. Femoral and tibial bowing were noted at birth. Radiographs at 6 years showed slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, normal knee epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly. Other skeletal findings were irregular vertebral endplates, flattening of the acetabula, and irregularity of the medial distal femoral epiphyses. He also had midfacial hypoplasia and autoimmune hypothyroidism. He did not have cleft palate or pes planus. His intelligence was normal, and his growth parameters had been in the normal range. He was last reported at 12 years of age.

Two of the patients were from 1 family with a COL9A3 variant. All 6 patients were highly myopic, with congenital megalophthalmos and abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel, and all had sensorineural hearing loss. One patient had severe arthropathy. Nixon et al. (2019) noted that sensorineural hearing loss is more common and more severe in recessive than in dominant Stickler syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) reported a 3-year-old Russian boy, born to nonconsanguineous parents, with congenital hip dysplasia and congenital high bilateral myopia. He also had speech delay and grade 3-4 bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. His eye findings included vitreoretinal degeneration, with peripheral retinal pigment rearrangement and dystrophic foci, as well as vitreous floaters and a preretinal membrane. His electroretinogram was normal, and he had no retinal detachment. Radiography revealed mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. This included mild platyspondyly, kyphosis, spina bifida occulta of the sacral vertebrae, flattened and irregular femoral heads, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses. He had early-onset arthropathy of the lower limbs with joint pain, genu valgum, prominent knee joints, limited hip abduction, waddling gait, lumbar lordosis, planovalgus foot deformity, and long fingers. His facial features included a flattened nasal bridge, small nose, mild midface hypoplasia, and high palate. He did not have cleft palate, and his height was normal.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) reported 5 patients from 3 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome. The proband from family 1 was a 28-year-old woman and was the only affected child of 3 born to first-cousin parents. She had high myopia in both eyes, vitreoretinal degeneration with empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations, and retinal pigmentary changes. She also had severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss and unilateral absence of the frontal sinus on skull x-ray. Her other findings were knee pain, pes planus, genu valgum, low-set ears, short metacarpals with widened epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly of the thoracic spine. She did not have cleft palate, micrognathia, short stature, retinal detachment, or intellectual disability.

paragraphs.text: In family 3 of Rad et al. (2022), 2 of 4 children of first-cousin parents were affected: a boy aged 11.8 years and a girl aged 3.1 years. Both had myopia and congenital, moderate to severe, progressive sensorineural hearing impairment. X-ray and detailed examination showed spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia in both children. Both had pes planus, a depressed nasal bridge, and anteverted nares. Midface hypoplasia and downslanting palpebral fissures were more pronounced in the girl. The boy complained of knee joint pain, especially when running. He also had genu valgum, bowed tibia, short metacarpals, broad hallux, irregular femoral epiphyses, and flat acetabular roofs with flattened femoral heads. Neither child had cleft palate, and none of the individuals in the study showed signs of intellectual disability.
